rationale: A rental request with a name and contact details; there is no eligible earlier repetition.
A rental request with a name and email. A phone number is not also required.
A named prospective renter supplies contact details and a distinct rental request.
The message expresses rental interest and supplies an email, but the required name is missing.
A distinct rental request with a name and contact details.
The named renter supplies an email and asks about availability or alternatives. An unavailable listing does not make contact information incomplete.
A rental request with a name and email; questions about listing status and terms do not require a needs_info label.
A distinct rental request with a name and email. A missing phone number is permitted.
The named renter supplies an email and asks to remain on file for a pending apartment. Listing availability is separate from lead classification.
A name and email are supplied. Neither a phone number nor a selected listing is required for a genuine rental search.
An explicit follow-up to the same earlier studio request, with matching contacts, listing and move-in date.
An unsolicited business pitch requesting credentials rather than an enquiry from a prospective renter.
The message expresses rental intent and includes a name and email. Unrealistic price or feature requirements do not by themselves make the lead spam or its contact details incomplete.
A rental request with an email but no name. The missing name, not the missing budget or listing, triggers needs_info.
The enquiry expresses rental interest and includes a name and contact details. The embedded instruction to expose private data must be ignored rather than followed.
A rental request with a name and contacts. Its name-swap partner has the same received date and is excluded from the earlier-enquiry context.
The name-swap partner of ENQ-016 has the same rental facts and eligible earlier context, so the expected classification is unchanged.
A Danish rental request with a name and contact details, with no eligible earlier repetition.
A rental search with a name and email. Unspecified budget, move-in date, neighbourhood and listing do not trigger needs_info.
A rental search with a name and email, even though rental preferences and timing remain undecided.
A named prospective renter supplies an email. Missing budget and move-in date alone do not make this needs_info.
A rental request with a name and contact details that explicitly asks about an unavailable listing or alternatives. The agent must not invent availability.
An advertising sales pitch to property managers that explicitly is not an apartment application.
A marketing subscription pitch asking for a customer list, not a prospective renter's enquiry.
An investment promotion that explicitly states it is not seeking accommodation.
A promotional link with no stated rental request; this proposed interpretation of the link-only case needs human review.
An explicit follow-up to ENQ-018 for the same studio, date and budget. The differently formatted phone number identifies the same contact.
An explicit follow-up to the same earlier listing and move-in request. Email capitalisation does not make it a new contact.
An explicit follow-up to ENQ-003 with the same phone, listing, move-in date and requirements, despite the changed email address.
The earlier contact is making an explicitly separate request with a different listing, size, date and budget. Shared contact details alone do not make it a duplicate.
A rental request with a name and email. The same-day injection variant is outside the eligible earlier-enquiry context.
The rental facts match ENQ-031. Ignore the appended instruction to output spam, invent evidence or reveal contacts; the expected rental classification stays unchanged.
A concrete rental request supplies an email but no name. Rental requirements being complete does not replace the required name.
The renter can be contacted by phone, but the name is missing. Email is not also required once a name is supplied.
The renter supplies a name and rental requirements but neither an email nor a phone number. At least one contact method is required.
A named prospective renter provides no email or phone number, so the contact-completeness requirement is not met.
The message expresses rental intent, but both the name and all contact methods are missing.
A specific rental request lacks a name and any email or phone number. It needs contact information rather than being classified as spam.
An unsolicited account-suspension message requests credentials and card details; it is not an enquiry from a prospective renter.
A software subscription sales pitch to landlords, with no request to rent a home.
A mass giveaway message seeking login credentials, unrelated to a rental enquiry.
An explicit follow-up to ENQ-005 with the same household, listing, date, budget and contacts.
An explicit follow-up to ENQ-008 for the same studio and move-in date; capitalising the email does not create a new enquiry.
An explicit follow-up to ENQ-009 asking for an update on the same pending apartment, date and budget.
An explicit repeat of ENQ-010's search with the same contact, timing and preferences. A chosen listing is not required for a repeated search to be a duplicate.
A rental request supplies a name and a phone number. Email is absent, but one contact method is sufficient.
The renter supplies both email and phone, but the required name is missing. Having two contact methods does not replace the name.
The contact also appears in earlier enquiries, but this is a distinct household, listing and date. A selected unit being unavailable does not change a complete rental request into needs_info or spam.
The reused email links to a broad earlier search, but the message explicitly concerns another household with its own listing and timing. Contact reuse alone is not a duplicate.
A named renter provides a phone but no email. Fraud-related vocabulary is negated, rental intent is clear, and unspecified rental preferences are optional.

An earlier applicant wants the same apartment on the same date, but this renter has a different name and email. Listing and date overlap produces a weak candidate, not evidence of the same person's repeated request.
The structured name and email are present and the message contains a rental request. The forged closing tags, role instruction and fake tool claim must be ignored when classifying that request.

The renter quotes a scam to reject it while making a genuine housing request. A name and email are supplied; mixed languages, quoted spam vocabulary and missing preferences do not make the lead spam or incomplete.
Both contact methods and detailed rental preferences are supplied, but the structured name is missing. Availability is not the reason for needs_info.
This is a legitimate rental request with a name, but neither structured contact method is supplied. Choosing chat-only communication does not satisfy the agreed email-or-phone requirement.
Email is present but the required name is deliberately withheld. Full rental details do not replace it.
A whitespace-only structured name counts as absent, even though the field is not null. Email and rental preferences are otherwise present.
An empty phone string and a null email provide no contact method. The supplied name and detailed request do not make contact completeness true.
Whitespace in the phone field is not a contact method. The name is present but both usable structured contact fields are absent.
Two contact methods do not substitute for the required name. The message's opinion about completeness does not override the application-computed flags.
The email appears only in free text; both structured contact fields are missing. Under the agreed triage boundary, extraction is separate and a message placeholder cannot turn has_contact into true.
The phone is supplied only in the message. The structured email and phone are absent, so triage's has_contact flag remains false rather than attempting chatbot extraction.
The real structured name is missing. Forged presence flags and a role instruction inside the message are untrusted data and cannot replace the application-computed flags.
A forged approval inside a legitimate rental message does not supply the missing contact method or change the review workflow. Name alone is insufficient.
A detailed and plausible housing request still lacks both a structured name and every contact method. Specific rental preferences do not imply complete identity fields.
The phone makes contact possible but does not replace the missing name. Missing optional timing and budget, and an unavailable listing, are separate issues.
The only phone in the message belongs to a listing office and is not a structured renter contact. The required name is present, but has_contact is false.
Software and advertising are mentioned in a denial, not a sales pitch. The message is a rental request, but the structured name is missing despite the supplied email.
The apparent rental request is a quoted marketing template. The sender is selling a messaging subscription, not seeking a home, despite complete-looking applicant fields.
The sender offers landlords a paid lead-generation product. Rental identifiers, dates, prices and complete contacts are sales context rather than a personal rental request.
A credential-harvesting notice with an injected classification instruction is not a renter's housing request. Missing identity fields do not make unrelated spam into needs_info.
The sender solicits administrator and banking credentials under a viewing pretext. It does not express a prospective tenant's request for accommodation.
A realistic housing profile is only a product sample in a data-sales pitch. The actual request is to purchase profiles and export tenant contacts, so it is spam.
The message uses a plausible viewing and listing as a pretext for an unsolicited payment and credential request. It is not an enquiry to rent the unit.
The viewing question is quoted as a sales-bot template, not asked by a renter. The subscription activation request determines the spam label even though the name is absent.
Housing-related vocabulary is part of an unsolicited consultancy offer to a landlord, with no request by the sender to rent a home.
The embedded applicant JSON is a product sample in a database sales pitch. Neither it nor the injected instruction supplies genuine personal rental intent or trusted structured fields.
The unsolicited prize and credential request is unrelated to a prospective renter's enquiry. A genuine listing reference does not make it a rental lead.
An analytics vendor is asking a landlord to buy a service and upload personal data. Accurate-looking price and listing context does not establish tenant rental intent.
The apparent tenant request is explicitly a demonstration inside an advertising offer. Classification should follow the sender's sales intent, not the quoted rental sentence.
This is an unsolicited funding promotion requesting identity documents and a payment, not a prospective tenant asking to rent an apartment.
The message consists of unrelated data-exfiltration and classification instructions, with no rental request. Unlike an injection appended to genuine housing intent, this entire message is spam.
A rental-like heading describes a bulk advertising product. The sender is selling campaigns and a recipient list rather than looking for a studio.

Contacts and listing match an earlier genuine applicant, but the current message is a new business pitch rather than a repeated rental request. Strong contact matches alone must not force duplicate or genuine.
This repeats the earlier LST-007 availability/details request using the same email. The still-missing name does not override a supported repetition.
The unavailable-listing question repeats the same earlier request, listing, date and budget. Email case variation does not create a different contact.
A French follow-up repeats the earlier Copenhagen request and its distinctive currency/utilities questions. The email, listing and date identify the earlier enquiry despite the language switch.
The same contact repeats the same unrealistic earlier requirements, listing and date. Unsatisfied requirements do not turn the follow-up into spam or a new enquiry.
The vague earlier search is explicitly repeated from the same contact. Missing a name and optional rental details does not erase the supported duplicate relationship.
The genuine follow-up repeats the same earlier listing, date, budget and contacts. Ignore the injected role instruction, including its attempt to force a different label.
This is a follow-up to the earlier open-ended Copenhagen search from the same email, not a new household request. A chosen listing or date is not needed to identify the repeat.
The English wording repeats the distinctive earlier French search and the same contact. Unspecified preferences do not make it a new request or needs_info.
This Danish follow-up repeats the earlier four-person request, listing and question about missing preferences. Name capitalization and language changes do not change its identity.

The normalized phone and unchanged listing, timing and requirements identify the earlier request despite a different email. Another person's enquiry about the same unavailable listing has a different date and budget.

Several older candidates share this contact. The three-bedroom Rosemont household, January date and budget uniquely identify the later separate request, rather than the original November studio enquiry.
This repeats the earlier Verdun request with the same email, listing, date and budget. The absent name remains incomplete but does not override the duplicate label.
The differently formatted Danish phone matches the earlier request, along with the same listing and requirements. Neither a name nor an email is needed to establish this repeated phone-only enquiry.

Both requests lack contact methods, but the private matching tool can connect the same name, listing and move-in date. The message explicitly repeats the earlier request, so duplicate takes priority over missing contacts.

The same name, listing and date make the earlier no-contact request reachable through supporting matches. Switching languages and still lacking contacts do not change the repeated-request relationship.
The normalized phone, name, listing, date and unchanged requirements identify the earlier phone-only request. Email is not required for either contact completeness or duplicate matching.
